page.name: Travel & hospitality
page.metaDescription: Booking confirmations, check-in links, arrival information and disruption alerts over the messaging accounts you already own.
page.lede: Travel messaging is shaped by the clock: a confirmation that has to arrive immediately, a reminder the evening before, a disruption notice that is worthless once the guest has left for the airport. Send each one from an account that is still accepting traffic.

bullets: Day-of arrival time and access information

sections.h: The one day you cannot afford a second failure
p: A disruption notice goes out when something has already gone wrong, which is the worst moment to discover that one provider account has stopped accepting traffic. On the SMS channel the platform can route to another connected account instead of failing, and normalized receipts show what actually left.
bullets: Automatic failover between your connected SMS accounts
Delivery receipts normalized into one status
Per-number pacing so a wide disruption send does not stall

p: Guest consent, the accuracy of the information you send and any local rules about contacting travelers are your responsibility. The platform carries the message, not the decision to send it.

faq.q: Can a message go out in the guest’s own language?
faq.a: Content is whatever you send, so any language the channel supports is possible. Non-Latin scripts change message segmentation, which affects message count and therefore cost.

faq.q: What if a guest replies to a disruption notice?
faq.a: Replies are captured as inbound messages and can be surfaced, but the platform is not a guest-services inbox. Route replies to your own system if you need to act on them.

faq.q: Can we send on WhatsApp as well as SMS?
faq.a: You can connect the accounts you hold on each channel and choose which one carries a given message. Routing and automatic failover are implemented for SMS; opt-out suppression applies to marketing sends on every channel, and receipts are normalized wherever the provider reports them.
